Comment raconter la guerre ? Comment rac: How do you tell the story of war? How do you tell of the horror, the deepest despair, the uprooting? How do you tell of the panic, the children hardened too quickly, the exhaustion of women who forget themselves, body and soul, for their families?
Comment raconter la guerre depuis l’inté: How do you tell the story of war from the inside, from its dark and winding bowels? How do you tell of the nuance, the emotional roller coaster? How do you tell of the small joys of daily life that make you forget the horror, if only for an hour? The shawarma you treat yourself to, those children’s smiles. Those little moments that make time pass pleasantly. How do you tell of the breath that catches with every new strike, the tight chest while watching the news, the grimaces when videos or images of destruction and mutilated bodies appear?
Comment faire comprendre ? Comment mettr: How do you make people understand? How do you put words to the unspeakable? How do I do my job with even more ethics and gentleness? How do I build trust when I’m suspected of being a spy?
En tant que journaliste étrangère au Lib: As a foreign journalist in Lebanon, I also had to deal with the pressure of journalism abroad. Correspondents are subject to a frantic pace to follow the news and report it. There’s no time to think, to cry or to stop and catch your breath. You have to cover everything that happens, whatever it takes. You’ll deal with your trauma later. Even though I don’t define myself as a news reporter, I felt that pressure too at the start of the escalation. And this while I live in Tripoli, 60 km from the attacks. After two days of shock and numbness, I remembered where my strengths and weaknesses lie. So I decided to work on displaced people, who became a major humanitarian issue a few days later.
Dans ce contexte, travailler est à la fo: In this context, working is both an ordeal and a form of therapy. Writing lets me vent everything the population is going through, but concentrating is very difficult. My phone is constantly on; I, too, spend my time following the news, checking in on my loved ones there and answering those who are worried from abroad. My nights are also short and restless, and every day I see my friends’ faces sag with fatigue and anguish. Their pain is indescribable. They are watching their country being destroyed, and their loved ones and fellow citizens being attacked. At the start of the escalation, a friend told me: “I’ve lost my youth, I’ve lost my future.” After years of study, of sacrifice, years of pandemic, then economic crisis, he has no hope left for his country. He never wanted to leave, but now he is forced to if he wants to live decently.
Dans cet article, je vous raconte un fra: In this article, I share a fragment of life in Lebanon and of the daily lives of Lebanese, Syrians and Palestinians. Above all, I am trying to keep the promise I made to every displaced person I met by putting faces to the numbers and political analyses.
Un an après le 7 octobre, le cauchemar c: One year after October 7, the nightmare continues and, above all, is growing. After 12 months of enduring cross-border fire between Hezbollah and the Israeli army, Lebanon’s population is facing a bloody escalation. More than 2,000 people have been killed and 9,800 wounded, and one million have been forced to leave their homes. Since September 17 and the explosion of Hezbollah members’ electronic devices, the country has been terrified and exhausted. This humanitarian crisis comes after a succession of already heavy economic and political crises. Whether they are in the heart of Beirut, in Tripoli, or in Canada thousands of kilometres away, Lebanese people have been holding their breath for three weeks. Their lives have been interrupted by relentless bombings and a death toll that keeps rising. For La Converse, they tell the unspeakable. Report.
Un an après l’attaque du 7 octobre par l: One year after Hamas’s October 7 attack, the mood in Lebanon is bleak. No one quite realizes it, but its people have been witnessing horrors for a year. What’s more, for the past three weeks the country and its diaspora have not been sleeping, overwhelmed by the escalating conflict in the country and Israel’s daily bombings.
Le dos est courbé, les yeux brûlent en r: Backs are hunched, eyes burn from lack of sleep, from hours spent staring at a small phone screen to follow the news every moment and stay in touch with loved ones. Since September 23, 2024, Lebanese people’s lives have been set to the rhythm of drones, bombings, and a count of the dead, the wounded and the destruction that piles up endlessly. This is their daily life. Whether they are in Lebanon or abroad.
« Depuis que je suis arrivée, je suis co: “Since I got back, I’ve been glued to my cellphone, watching the news and writing to my family,” confides Michelle from her Montréal apartment. She preferred not to disclose her identity. “You can keep my first name, because I want Canadians to be surprised to see an Arab woman with a familiar name!” she tells me, laughing, during our WhatsApp call. Born in Canada, she is also Lebanese. She has just returned from her annual stay with her family, in a village not far from Tripoli, in the north of the small country. “It’s a safe place, but all the young people work in Beirut during the week. I’m very worried about them. It’s hard,” continues the professional dancer.
La jeune femme aux longs cheveux bouclés: The young woman, with long curly hair dyed purple, went to Lebanon to spend the summer and celebrate three weddings. Her return flight was scheduled for September 24, a few days after the simultaneous explosions of electronic devices and the bloody bombings that followed. After several flight cancellations, she managed to leave on the 29th, the day before the assassination of Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah. “I felt a strong sense of guilt about getting out. I left, but the others, my loved ones, can’t. If I hadn’t had to go back for work, I wouldn’t have minded being there,” she says. Like many Lebanese people, she would rather be with her family than safe abroad.
Des familles déplacées de la banlieue su: Displaced families from Beirut’s southern suburbs, settled on the steps of the Grand Al-Amine Mosque, wait to be relocated to emergency shelters. Beirut (Lebanon), 28/09/2024. Photo: Philippe Pernot
Pourtant, et Michelle le sait bien, être: And yet, as Michelle knows well, being in Lebanon means being confronted with the news, with the sound of bombs every night, with the sound of drones several hours a day and with Israeli planes flying over the country from north to south. All of it feeds the psychological warfare. “I arrived in July, when Israeli army aircraft were starting to break the sound barrier over Beirut and in the south almost every day. It’s a tactic to terrorize people,” the young woman explains. Causing a loud blast, similar to an explosion, this manoeuvre makes the war impossible to forget. Just like the drones and their propeller-plane noise.
Depuis son retour à Montréal, elle préfè: Since returning to Montréal, she prefers to drown herself in work rather than think. “I haven’t reconnected with my emotions. It’s as if I feel nothing,” she says.
Comme Michelle, Marie* n’a d’autre choix: Like Michelle, Marie* has no choice but to keep working and carry on with a normal life. And this while Israel pounds Lebanon once night falls, terrorizing those in the country and paralyzing those far away. A permanent resident for a year, she left Lebanon in a hurry when the war broke out in 2023. Back in the country for two weeks in September, she escaped the worst by returning to Canada before the conflict escalated.
« Certaines personnes me disent que je s: “Some people tell me I’m lucky to have left. Yes, I left the country, but I’m sick of watching the bombings on my country, of seeing the victims,” Marie snaps. “Even when you’re not in Lebanon, you’re constantly frozen in front of your screens, you have insomnia. We’re unable to cry, we’ve already used up our tears for Palestine, and we’ve been seeing horrible images every day for a year.” She feels the same guilt as Michelle and other Lebanese people abroad: “Many are stuck in Lebanon! It’s too much to handle,” she sighs.
Depuis l’étranger, ces femmes partagent: From abroad, these women share the terror caused by the bombings and the short nights spent following the news: the latest neighbourhoods or buildings hit, the citizen and community mobilization to support the million displaced people seeking safety, the exhaustion and horror on the road for those fleeing from south to north.
Après un week-end sanglant de bombardeme: After a bloody weekend of bombings across the entire south of the country, hundreds of thousands of people fled the region to seek refuge in Beirut or farther north. They joined the 110,000 people who had been fleeing the southern border for months to cities farther north, such as Tyre or Sidon.
Ce lundi 23 septembre, Salwa* n’a pas ré: On Monday, September 23, Salwa* didn’t think for long. She fled with her children, Mira* and Ali*, to take shelter in an abandoned hotel in Tripoli, the country’s second-largest city, 60 km north of Beirut. Reluctantly, they had to leave their home in Nabatieh, 70 km southeast of Beirut.
Une famille déplacée de la banlieue sud: A displaced family from Beirut’s southern suburbs, settled on the steps of the Grand Al-Amine Mosque, receives sandwiches from volunteers. Beirut (Lebanon), 28/09/2024. Photo: Philippe Pernot
« Dès que nous avons entendu le bruit de: “As soon as we heard the sound of the warplanes, we started packing. We literally arrived in slippers. People were crying and screaming. Mom started moaning on the ground. There was broken glass everywhere,” says their daughter Mira, sitting in the grass next to Ali, her younger brother. She is only 13 and talks about the bombs and the planes breaking the sound barrier as if she had known it all her life, as if she were 20 years older. She is self-assured and unflinchingly describes the horror they have endured day and night since the pager attack in their city: “Since then, the attacks have come every day. We barely slept because of the noise of the Israeli jets breaking the sound barrier.”
Je les rencontre dans le jardin de l’hôt: I meet them in the hotel garden. They arrived three days ago. There, the sound of the wind in the orange trees and the birdsong mingle with the children’s cries. Right next to it, cars come and go delivering goods and supplies. Volunteers and refugees bustle around the hotel entrance to organize aid and support the 1,000 people staying in the hotel. It took just 24 hours for the building to fill up, like the fifty or so other shelters scattered across Tripoli and its surroundings.
Le 23 septembre, la panique était totale: On September 23, the panic was total and the blocked roads looked apocalyptic. Mira has only one word to describe it: “Horror.” A trip that normally takes an hour could easily take all day. “It took us 10 hours. It was a nightmare, with lots of rockets, warplanes and smoke,” adds Salwa, quieter than her daughter.

Quelques jours plus tard, alors que la s: A few days later, while the situation is still chaotic, Israel relentlessly bombs Beirut’s southern suburbs. Since then, the neighbourhood has been bombed almost daily. So much so that an entire suburb has nearly emptied of its 500,000 residents. Tens of thousands have taken refuge in the streets, settling on the seaside corniche, on the beach, in parks or on the famous Martyrs’ Square. Since then, their numbers have dropped, and most have found more permanent shelter, rented an apartment or been taken in by family members.
Mais, deux semaines plus tard, des homme: But two weeks later, men, women and children are still sleeping outside, for lack of space in the shelters.
Après une nuit entrecoupée par le bruit: After a night broken up by the sound of 17 bombs dropped on several neighbourhoods of the city, I head to Ramlet al-Baïda (“white sand” in Arabic), Beirut’s public beach, to meet displaced people. It is October 3 and, like every morning for three weeks, Beirut wakes up in rough shape. People no longer ask how you are, but how you slept or how you’re surviving.
Des tentes installées sur la plage publi: Tents set up on the Ramlet al-Bayda public beach shelter displaced families from South Lebanon. Beirut (Lebanon), 28/09/2024. Photo: Philippe Pernot
Ce matin-là, le soleil de midi est éblou: That morning, the midday sun is dazzling and crushing. Children play in the water and on the swings, their skin already well tanned from the week they have spent here. Meanwhile, the adults shelter from the sun in rickety huts. A group of women sit in a circle smoking hookah and chatting. The setting could be idyllic if not for the war, if these beachgoers hadn’t lost everything because of it and the Israeli bombings.
Je m’installe à côté de ce petit groupe: I sit down next to this small group facing the sea. Most are Syrians who fled the war in their own country more than 10 years ago. Just last week, they were still living in Beirut’s southern suburbs. Their faces are tired, their skin is dry, and one man’s body is covered in rashes from the lack of hygiene. “I left last week with my two children. We’ve been living outside for 10 days,” explains Fatema, mother of two boys. A scarf covers her hair, dyed blond. After “selling everything” to leave Syria, she got by on several odd jobs. Now, she has no income.
Désespérée et révoltée, elle prend le té: Desperate and outraged, she takes the phone, which records her words, to get her message out to the world and denounce the situation in Lebanon to the West. “I have nothing left! No more money, no more home, nothing. All I have left is this bag of clothes for two boys,” she says, pointing at the plastic bag beside her.
Chaque jour, elle amène ses enfants à la: Every day, she brings her children to Beirut’s public beach to keep them occupied. All she wants is money to go back to Syria. Above all, she wants to get her children out of this misery. “The children cry constantly. Their father is their only support, and he’s in Syria, injured and without income for a year. My family is in Turkey,” she laments. The day before, she had to celebrate her son’s birthday without being able to give him a present. “He’s 11, but we didn’t really celebrate,” she says regretfully.
Powerless, Fatema can only wait. Like the million other displaced people. While some have been able to rent a new place, others are squeezed into other families’ homes. Around 115,000 people are reportedly housed in nearly 900 shelters, in precarious conditions, sometimes without water or electricity. These shelters have been set up in schools – which won’t be able to reopen for some time –, community centres or hotels. And then there are those who, like Fatema, are still on the street. Around 185,000 people have also reportedly crossed into neighbouring Syria.
En remontant les escaliers depuis la pla: Climbing the stairs from the beach to the road, you can see families set up behind tarps and blankets on the sidewalk. They hide from the sun and try to find some semblance of privacy. For now, these makeshift shelters work, because the weather is still mild. But winter is approaching, and with it storms, wind, rain and, above all, cold. Associations visit them daily to assess their needs and provide some support. “We get food every day, at least once a day, thank God,” says Fatema.
Mais cette aide d’urgence n’est pas viab: But this emergency aid is not sustainable in a country whose population is already overwhelmed by a succession of political and economic crises. Indeed, Lebanon has had no government for more than two years and is going through one of the worst economic crises since 1850. The consequences include hyperinflation – turning everyday products into luxury goods –, a 98% devaluation of the Lebanese pound and wages that haven’t kept up, leaving many Lebanese people earning only $70 to $140 a month.
Face à cette situation dramatique qui pr: Faced with this dramatic situation, which has triggered yet another crisis, a humanitarian one this time, the whole country has mobilized. In addition to shelters, restaurants and community spaces have been turned into soup kitchens. NGOs and local associations have put their work on hold to respond to the emergency and distribute mattresses, clothing, food and hygiene kits for women and children. Citizens are also mobilizing, providing supplies and pitching in as volunteers.
Des enfants d’une famille déplacée de la: Children from a displaced family from Beirut’s southern suburbs play on suitcases in front of the Grand Al-Amine Mosque. Beirut (Lebanon), 28/09/2024. Photo: Philippe Pernot
« Pour l’instant, il y a beaucoup d’init: “For now, there are a lot of civilian initiatives to support displaced people, but we need something permanent, and that’s what we’re starting to put in place,” explains Jad Al Rayess, of the NGO Operation Big Blue, whom I met on the beach. And what will happen when those who are helping have spent too many nights without sleep? When they, too, need help because a bomb has exploded in their neighbourhood, and they too have to flee?
Plus que de l’aide, les personnes déplac: More than aid, the displaced people I met mostly want to show the world what is happening in Lebanon. They are demanding justice and the support of the international community as well as the Arab world. Having lost everything, not all of them have the privilege of being able to start living again in another city or another country. Most are condemned to wait. To wait to go back to school, to wait to work again, to wait to return to their region and rebuild themselves.
« Si j’ai l’occasion de rentrer dans le: “If I get the chance to go back to the south, I will,” says Ali defiantly. Despite his smile and provocative tone, his joke says a lot about his real motivation: to get back his life, his region and his home. To go back to school and have the life a 10-year-old should have. The life he had before October 8.
